appraisal_events.evidence: She speaks of the new people she meets as 'trophées chèrement achetés' ('Rapporté d'une Expédition chez les un Tel'); Mme Swann 'n'avait obtenu de résultats que dans ce qu'on appelait le monde officiel. Les femmes élégantes n'allaient pas chez elle'; and she is shown confusing dukes and princes ('ceux-là sont princes, ils ont donc monté en grade') and misplacing the Guermantes' province ('de l'Aisne').
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator sustains an ironic, unflattering portrait of Odette's calculated social climbing and exposes her comic ignorance of the aristocratic codes she claims to have mastered, diminishing her despite her social ambitions.

appraisal_events.evidence: Lady Israels used her influence 'à ce qu'aucune personne qu'elle connaissait ne reçût Odette'; when Mme de Marsantes disobeyed and Lady Israels arrived during Odette's visit, Mme de Marsantes, 'avec la lâcheté des gens qui pourtant pourraient tout se permettre,' 'n'adressa pas une fois la parole à Odette,' discouraging any further incursion into that world.
appraisal_events.explanation: Odette is concretely excluded and publicly ignored: Lady Israels' organized social blockade and Mme de Marsantes' cowardly refusal to acknowledge her jointly bar Odette from the Faubourg Saint-Germain.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's sustained irony over her trophy-hunting sociability and her ignorance of basic aristocratic distinctions locally lowers Odette's standing.
Odette is actively and effectively barred from the elite social world she aspires to, both by Lady Israels' campaign and by Mme de Marsantes' refusal to acknowledge her.
The narrator explicitly frames her silence toward Odette as cowardice ('la lâcheté des gens qui pourtant pourraient tout se permettre'), locally lowering her despite her high rank.
